clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in DDHD1 on chromosome 14, which encodes the intracellular phospholipase A1 known as PA-PLA1.
Usually early or childhood-onset, slowly progressive and relatively pure spastic paraparesis.
A subclinical axonal, predominantly sensory, neuropathy is frequently found on nerve conduction studies despite an apparently pure clinical picture.
Cerebellar oculomotor signs, such as saccadic pursuit and impaired vestibulo-ocular reflex suppression, are recognised subtle complicating features.
It belongs to the phospholipase-related HSP group together with SPG54 (DDHD2), both of which disturb membrane phospholipid metabolism.
Brain MRI is often normal, whereas MR spectroscopy may reveal an abnormal cerebral lipid signal, a finding more marked in the allied DDHD2-related SPG54.
Distinguish it from SPG54 (DDHD2), which is typically more complicated with cognitive impairment, a thin corpus callosum and a prominent spectroscopic lipid peak.
Management is symptomatic, and there is no disease-modifying therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG28 is an autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in DDHD1 at chromosome 14q22.1. DDHD1 encodes phosphatidic acid-preferring phospholipase A1 (PA-PLA1), an intracellular phospholipase A1 that hydrolyses membrane glycerophospholipids, notably phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol, thereby regulating the pools of lysophospholipids and free fatty acids that govern membrane curvature, organelle dynamics and lipid signalling. Loss of DDHD1 activity is thought to disturb phospholipid and mitochondrial homeostasis within long central motor neurons, causing the characteristic length-dependent dying-back degeneration of the corticospinal tracts, with additional distal peripheral axonal, particularly sensory, involvement. DDHD1 belongs to the same intracellular phospholipase A1 family as DDHD2 (mutated in SPG54) and SEC23IP, which helps explain the overlapping phenotypes and the abnormal cerebral lipid accumulation detectable by MR spectroscopy within this group. The gene product's role in phosphoinositide turnover and membrane trafficking links SPG28 to the broader theme of disrupted lipid metabolism and organelle shaping seen across many HSP subtypes.
additionalDifferentials: SPG54 (DDHD2) - the pathway sibling, typically more complicated with a spectroscopic lipid peak and thin corpus callosum
SPG24 and SPG27 - other autosomal recessive early-onset subtypes
SPG7 (paraplegin) - common recessive HSP with possible cerebellar and ocular signs
SPG11 (spatacsin) - recessive HSP with a thin corpus callosum and cognitive decline
PNPLA6-related disorders (including Boucher-Neuhauser syndrome) - other lipid-metabolism HSPs
Hereditary sensory and motor neuropathy - given the subclinical peripheral neuropathy
Dopa-responsive dystonia and other treatable mimics of childhood spastic gait
additionalInvestigations: Targeted DDHD1 sequencing or a next-generation sequencing HSP gene panel with confirmation of biallelic variants
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to detect the subclinical axonal sensory neuropathy
MRI of brain and spinal cord, which is often normal but excludes structural and demyelinating disease and a thin corpus callosum
MR spectroscopy to look for an abnormal cerebral lipid signal within the DDHD-related group
Oculomotor and vestibular assessment for cerebellar eye-movement abnormalities
Metabolic screen including very-long-chain fatty acids and plasma amino acids to exclude mimics
redFlags: Rapid progression or a sensory level suggesting a compressive or structural cord lesion rather than HSP
Prominent cognitive decline or seizures suggesting SPG54 or another complicated HSP
Systemic or metabolic features suggesting an inborn error of metabolism
Acute rather than insidious onset of bladder dysfunction
reference.prognosis: SPG28 is slowly progressive and often remains relatively pure, and many patients maintain ambulation with walking aids over many years. It is generally milder and more slowly progressive than the allied DDHD2-related SPG54, and no curative therapy is available.
pitfalls: Labelling the disorder as pure HSP and not performing nerve conduction studies, thereby missing the subclinical neuropathy
Confusing SPG28 (DDHD1) with SPG54 (DDHD2), which share a mechanism but differ in severity and imaging
Expecting an abnormal MRI, since normal structural imaging does not exclude SPG28
Overlooking the diagnostic value of MR spectroscopy in the DDHD-related group
